clinicalPearls: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones form only in urine infected by urease-producing organisms, classically Proteus mirabilis and also Klebsiella, Pseudomonas and Ureaplasma
The enzyme urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, alkalinising the urine and supplying the ammonium and carbonate needed for crystallisation
These are the archetypal stones that grow rapidly and fill the collecting system as staghorn calculi
They occur more often in women and in patients with recurrent urinary infection, neurogenic bladder, indwelling catheters or urinary diversion
A persistently alkaline urine with recurrent urea-splitting organisms is an important diagnostic clue
Coffin-lid shaped crystals may be seen on urine microscopy
Cure requires complete surgical clearance of every fragment, because residual material harbours bacteria and seeds regrowth
Culture-directed antibiotics against the urease organism, sometimes with a urease inhibitor and urinary acidification, support treatment but cannot substitute for complete stone clearance
reference.pathophysiology: Struvite stones are a direct consequence of chronic urinary infection with bacteria that produce urease. Urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide; the ammonia raises the urine pH and generates ammonium while carbon dioxide yields carbonate. In this persistently alkaline environment magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) and carbonate apatite become supersaturated and precipitate rapidly, frequently incorporating bacteria within the stone matrix. Because organisms are sequestered inside the stone, infection cannot be eradicated by antibiotics alone, and any retained fragment allows the process to recur and the stone to enlarge.
additionalDifferentials: Calcium stones forming a staghorn configuration
Uric acid stone with secondary infection
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT to define the stone burden and staghorn configuration
Urine culture to identify the urease-producing organism and guide antibiotics
Urine pH, which is characteristically alkaline, and microscopy for crystals
Stone analysis confirming struvite and carbonate apatite composition
Serum renal function and, in bilateral disease, assessment of split renal function
Metabolic evaluation to exclude a coexisting metabolic stone nidus
redFlags: Sepsis arising from an infected obstructed system
Rapid staghorn growth threatening renal function
Progressive loss of function in the affected kidney
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis that may require nephrectomy
reference.prognosis: If every fragment is cleared and infection eradicated, cure is achievable; incomplete clearance leads to a high recurrence rate, and long-standing staghorn calculi can destroy renal function and, rarely, are associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the collecting system.
pitfalls: Treating with antibiotics alone and expecting cure without complete stone removal
Leaving residual fragments that reseed both infection and stone
Missing a coexisting metabolic abnormality that acted as the initial nidus
Underestimating the sepsis risk when instrumenting an infected stone
management: Definitive complete surgical stone clearance, principally percutaneous nephrolithotomy for staghorn calculi, aiming for a wholly stone-free state
Culture-directed antibiotics to treat the associated urinary infection perioperatively, recognising that antibiotics alone cannot eradicate organisms sequestered within the stone
Consider urease inhibition with acetohydroxamic acid in selected patients unfit for surgery or with unavoidable residual stone
Address predisposing factors: manage neurogenic bladder, change or remove indwelling catheters, and relieve urinary stasis and obstruction
Surveillance imaging and urine culture for residual fragments and recurrence given rapid regrowth from any retained nidus
Metabolic evaluation to identify and treat a coexisting metabolic stone-forming tendency
Nephrectomy considered for a non-functioning, chronically infected kidney, with urology referral for operative planning
